# Image generation with imagegen

The image tools follow reference pixels better than prose. Each call has three parts: references that carry look and geometry, a prompt that carries structure and facts, and a check of the file that came back. The tool descriptions list their arguments and limits. Where a backend registers separate tools for creating from text and for editing existing images, create with `imagegen` and edit with `imageedit`, and use the model information tool it offers (`imagegen_models`) to choose a model instead of guessing one.

## Pick the medium

Icons, logos, charts, diagrams, and anything that must scale, be recoloured or be edited later belong in SVG or code, or in an existing icon set. Generate rasters for photos, illustrations, textures and visual concepts. When a layout needs exact positions, spacing or small text, render it in code and pass the render as a reference.

## Write the call

- Label each reference by role in the prompt: "Image 1: approved style; copy its colours and shadows. Image 2: layout at true size; match positions." Say what to borrow and what to leave out.
- Pass geometry as a picture (a rendered layout, a crop, a sketch). Dimensions written in words come out approximate.
- Order the prompt: medium and framing, the role of each reference, content in reading order with every visible string in quotes, then hard constraints. For an app screen, state "flat screen capture, no device frame".
- Assign colour by role and name where colour must not appear; otherwise labels and states get colour-coded on their own.
- Pick the size or aspect ratio that fits the use.

## Correct

Pass the result back as a reference and write: "Reproduce Image 1 faithfully: same layout, scale, colours and text. Apply only these corrections: 1. ... 2. ..." Name the region and the exact new values. Batch every fix for an image into one round, because each regeneration can change things you did not mention. Compare the result with the previous version, not only against the requested fix.

A reference-guided edit regenerates the whole image. When a region must stay pixel-identical, or one region keeps failing, edit or composite locally and record that the image was patched.

## Keep related images consistent

Approve one anchor image first, then pass it as the style reference for each sibling and label its role. Separate generations drift in layout and detail, so frames that must match each other, such as a storyboard or a before-and-after pair, may be better generated as one numbered grid and cut afterwards.

## Exact text

Large headings usually render correctly; small text can pick up misspellings. When wording matters, leave it out of the generated image and draw it afterwards in code.

## Transparency

Set `background` to `transparent` for an isolated cut-out and ask for one subject with clear margin on every side. The returned alpha can be soft at the edges and across the subject, so process it when a hard cut-out or fully opaque subject is needed. Recheck the alpha after every correction round; do not assume an edit kept it.

## Check and record

- Open every result at full size and crop dense regions. Read the pixel size the tool reports instead of assuming the requested size.
- Check each quoted string, the colour roles, everything the prompt forbade, and anything that changed without being asked.
- For transparency, check the image mode and alpha, and view the result on a light and a dark background.
- Report what the final file is: which images were generated, from which references, and any post-processing such as upscaling, patching or matting. Say so when a result was not checked or differs from the request.

# oc-multi-imagegen [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/oc-multi-imagegen)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/oc-multi-imagegen) Generate and edit images without leaving OpenCode. Describe what you need, give your agent a reference when you have one, and get an image saved in your project. Use your OpenCode ChatGPT sign-in with the default **Codex backend**, or connect an OpenAI Images API or NanoGPT key. The plugin works in OpenCode 1 and OpenCode 2 and includes a skill that guides agents through prompting, reference images and checking the result. **[Examples](#from-a-prompt-to-a-finished-asset) · [Get started](#get-started) · [Backends](#choose-a-backend) · [Documentation](#documentation)** ## What you can make - **Illustrations from a prompt:** scene art, website imagery, textures and visual concepts. - **Variations from references:** change the weather, restyle an image or combine several images in one request. - **Transparent assets:** turn a character or object into a cut-out for an avatar, sticker or illustrated icon. - **Images your agent can keep working with:** each result is a local PNG, ready to inspect, reference in another call or use in your project. ## From a prompt to a finished asset These original, Ghibli-inspired illustrations were generated through the Codex backend. Each step builds on the image before it. The prompts below show how to ask your agent; the [full prompts and settings](docs/examples.md) are available too. ### 1. Describe a scene > Create a hand-painted woodland post office inside an enormous old tree, with a mossy roof, a stone bridge and warm afternoon light. A little fox postmaster in a teal raincoat carries a letter. Give it the quiet wonder of a Ghibli-inspired animation background. Save it as `forest-post-office.png`. ![A fox postmaster on a stone bridge outside a tree-house post office, overlooking a sunlit mountain lake.](docs/images/forest-post-office.webp) You don't need to name a tool or write a JSON request. Your agent turns the description into an `imagegen` call and saves the result. ### 2. Give it a reference and a new direction > Use `forest-post-office.png` as a reference. Keep the post office, bridge and fox, but make it a rainy blue-hour scene with glowing amber windows and reflections on the wet stone. Save it as `forest-post-office-rain.png`. ![The same woodland post office and fox at rainy blue hour, with amber windows and wet reflections.](docs/images/forest-post-office-rain.webp) On Codex, adding `images` makes the same tool perform a reference-guided edit. Name what to keep and what to change; edits generate a new image, so they aren't pixel-exact patches. ### 3. Pull out a reusable character > Use `forest-post-office-rain.png` as a reference. Turn the fox postmaster into a standalone illustrated icon. Keep the teal coat, mail satchel, bell and envelope. Show the whole character on a transparent background, without the scenery or a drop shadow. Save it as `fox-postmaster-icon.png`. The agent supplies the reference and sets `background: "transparent"`. This PNG has real transparency, checked on light and dark backgrounds. Fine edges and the character itself can have soft alpha; use a vector tool when you need an editable vector icon. ## Get started Add the npm package to your OpenCode configuration. OpenCode installs it when the server starts. **OpenCode 1** (`plugin`): ```json { "plugin": ["oc-multi-imagegen"] } ``` **OpenCode 2** (`plugins`): ```json { "plugins": ["oc-multi-imagegen"] } ``` Sign in to OpenCode with ChatGPT and restart the server that loads the plugin. Codex is the default, so it needs no backend setting or separate image API key. The [setup guide](docs/getting-started.md) covers authentication, version pinning and local development. Then ask for an image. The [permissions guide](docs/permissions.md) covers agents with restricted tool access. ## Choose a backend | Backend | Use it with | Image tools | | --- | --- | --- | | **Codex** (default) | Your OpenCode ChatGPT sign-in | `imagegen` for generation and reference edits | | **OpenAI Images API** | An OpenAI image API key | `imagegen` with native pixel sizes | | **NanoGPT** | A NanoGPT API key | Separate generation/editing tools and a choice of curated models | [Backend setup and model choices](docs/backends.md) explain authentication, controls and availability. Generation uses the selected provider's account quota or API credit. NanoGPT support is covered by mocked tests and hasn't been validated with live calls. ## Documentation | Guide | What you'll find | | --- | --- | | [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | Installation, ChatGPT sign-in and configuration for both OpenCode hosts | | [Examples](docs/examples.md) | Full prompts, reference chain and settings behind the images above | | [Backends](docs/backends.md) | Codex, OpenAI and NanoGPT setup, credentials and model selection | | [Tool reference](docs/tool-reference.md) | Arguments, sizes, references, transparency and output behavior | | [Permissions](docs/permissions.md) | Agent access, backend-scoped rules and file access | | [Development](docs/development.md) | Build, test, packaging and compatibility details | | [Container testing](https://github.com/imarshallwidjaja/oc-multi-imagegen/blob/main/docs/container-testing.md) | Source-checkout runbook for live tests with real agents | ## License [MIT](LICENSE). The original copyright and permission notice are retained.

# Backends

[README](../README.md) · [Getting started](getting-started.md) · [Tool reference](tool-reference.md)

One backend is active per plugin load. The selected backend controls the registered tools, their arguments and their defaults.

| `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_BACKEND` | Provider | Credential | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unset or `codex` | ChatGPT Codex image backend | OpenCode's ChatGPT sign-in for `openai` | `imagegen` |
| `openai-api` | Official OpenAI Images API | `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_OPENAI_API_KEY`, otherwise saved `openai-images` key | `imagegen` |
| `nano-gpt` | NanoGPT normalized image API | `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_NANOGPT_API_KEY`, otherwise saved `nano-gpt-images` key | `imagegen`, `imageedit`, `imagegen_models` |

Changing the backend takes a server restart. A call can't select another backend, and a failure doesn't trigger a retry or fallback to another backend.

## Configuration

The plugin reads three environment variables:

| Variable | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_BACKEND` | Read once at plugin load. Empty or unknown values fail the load without registering image tools. |
| `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_OPENAI_API_KEY` | Image key for `openai-api` only, resolved on each call. |
| `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_NANOGPT_API_KEY` | Image key for `nano-gpt` only, resolved on each call. |

The plugin takes no options and reads no `.env` or other configuration file. Remove a `backend` option left by an older build; it now fails the load with a message naming the environment variable to use. Other plugin options also fail.

Set variables in the environment of the OpenCode **server**. Exporting one in a shell that only starts a client attached to a running server doesn't change that server's environment.

### systemd example

For a system service named `opencode.service`, an OpenAI API configuration can use:

```ini
[Service]
Environment=OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_BACKEND=openai-api
EnvironmentFile=/etc/opencode/oc-multi-imagegen.env
```

The environment file contains a placeholder here; store the real file with mode `600`:

```sh
OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_OPENAI_API_KEY=<OpenAI Images API key>
```

Run `systemctl daemon-reload` and `systemctl restart opencode.service` after changing the unit or its environment file. For a user unit, use `systemctl --user daemon-reload` and `systemctl --user restart opencode.service`, with an environment file you own, such as `%h/.config/opencode/oc-multi-imagegen.env`.

Use `nano-gpt` and `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_NANOGPT_API_KEY` for NanoGPT. Keep keys in restricted environment files rather than readable unit files. These files are read by systemd, not by the plugin.

## Codex

Codex uses OpenCode's ChatGPT sign-in. Access depends on your account and the availability and limits of the ChatGPT Codex image backend; an OpenAI API key doesn't authenticate it.

- **OpenCode 1** reads the `openai` OAuth entry from `OPENCODE_AUTH_CONTENT` when set, otherwise from `auth.json` under OpenCode's XDG data directory.
- **OpenCode 2** resolves the active `openai` connection on every call. It accepts **Codex browser (legacy)** and **Codex device code (legacy)**, with the connection's account ID when present. It rejects the **Sign in with ChatGPT** token-sharing method, API keys, missing connections and unrecognized methods. Host credential lookup or refresh errors propagate unchanged.

OpenCode 2 doesn't read `OPENCODE_AUTH_CONTENT` or `auth.json`, and the plugin doesn't refresh OAuth tokens. Neither image API key variable affects Codex.

The default request names `gpt-image-2` with `quality: auto`. Model and quality overrides are sent as requested, but the Codex response doesn't identify the settings it applied. In a direct-request study on one ChatGPT Pro account on 2026-10-20, requests accepted nonexistent model names and didn't reliably honor requested quality tiers. Treat these controls as **requested, not verified**; a call using either override reports that distinction. See [sizes and output](tool-reference.md#sizes) for the similar distinction between requested and returned dimensions.

## OpenAI Images API

This backend uses a key separate from the `openai` chat provider. The plugin sends it only to OpenAI's `/v1/images/generations` or `/v1/images/edits` endpoint when an image is requested. Loading the plugin doesn't check the key or make a network request.

The request defaults to model `gpt-image-2.5-sunburst` and quality `auto`. Any `model` or `quality` string is passed through; the API decides whether the model exists, the key can use it and the settings are supported. API calls bill the key's account. HTTP errors include the status and response body, with the key removed.

### Key precedence

1. If `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_OPENAI_API_KEY` is **present**, it is the credential. A present empty value or a value unsuitable for an HTTP header fails the call without consulting a saved key. A rejected key is reported once, without trying another credential.
2. Otherwise, the plugin uses the `openai-images` key saved in OpenCode.

It never reads `OPENAI_API_KEY`, which might be a chat key, or loads a dotenv file.

### Save a key in OpenCode

- **OpenCode 1:** run `opencode auth login --provider openai-images`, or choose **Other** in the provider list and enter `openai-images`. The host saves an `api` entry. The plugin registers an API sign-in method, not a chat provider or model.
- **OpenCode 2:** run `opencode auth login openai-images`, or connect the **OpenAI Images API** integration. It registers key and environment methods. When the variable is present, the plugin asks the host to resolve that environment connection directly, even if the host lists a saved key first. Otherwise it resolves the active saved connection.

OpenCode 1 reads the variable itself after permission. Without it, it follows the host's stored-auth behavior: `OPENCODE_AUTH_CONTENT`, falling through to `auth.json` if that content doesn't parse. OpenCode 2 only checks variable presence and lets the host read the value; it never falls back to those files. Missing or non-key credentials produce a message naming the variable or sign-in command. Chat credentials are never used as an image key.

## NanoGPT

Select `nano-gpt` and provide `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_NANOGPT_API_KEY` in the server environment, or save a key under `nano-gpt-images`:

- **OpenCode 1:** `opencode auth login --provider nano-gpt-images`.
- **OpenCode 2:** `opencode auth login nano-gpt-images`, or connect the **NanoGPT API** integration.

Environment-over-saved precedence, failure behavior and per-host resolution work as for the OpenAI image key. The plugin doesn't read the other backends' keys, `NANOGPT_API_KEY` or dotenv files. It sends the key only to `https://api.nano-gpt.com/api/v1/images`. Result downloads carry no key.

### Generation and editing models

Every image call names an exact supported model ID. `imagegen` creates from text; `imageedit` requires references. Use the local `imagegen_models` tool to find the right model and its input schema without a key, file access or network request.

| Family | `imagegen` model | `imageedit` model | Optional controls | Edit references |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GPT Image 2.5 Flare | `openai/gpt-image-2.5/flare/text-to-image` | `openai/gpt-image-2.5/flare/edit` | `resolution`, `aspect_ratio`, `quality`, `background` | Up to 16 |
| Nano Banana Pro | `nano-banana-pro` | `nano-banana-pro-edit` | `resolution`, `aspect_ratio` | Up to 10 |
| FLUX.3 Image | `black-forest-labs/flux-3/text-to-image` | `black-forest-labs/flux-3/edit` | `resolution`, `aspect_ratio` | Up to 10 |
| Seedream 5.0 Pro | `bytedance/seedream-v5.0-pro` | `bytedance/seedream-v5.0-pro/edit` | `resolution`, including ratios such as `16:9` | Up to 10, each at most 10 MiB |
| Qwen Image 2.1 | `qwen-image-2.1/text-to-image` | `qwen-image-2.1/edit` | `resolution`, `aspect_ratio`, `seed` | Up to 10 |

Controls left out of a call aren't sent, so NanoGPT applies its defaults. An unsupported control, value, model, operation or unknown argument is rejected before a provider request. No generic passthrough or runtime catalogue fetch is provided; new NanoGPT models need an update to the plugin's table.

Agents are guided to respect the operator's model choice, otherwise pick a supported model and give a short reason. Missing inputs or conflicts with a requested model, capability, cost or requirement need the operator's decision. Errors never silently change a model. Authentication, balance and rate-limit failures aren't retried; an agent should only correct an input when the error identifies a demonstrable mistake.

The curated table follows NanoGPT documentation and public metadata, which are incomplete and inconsistent between sources. It **hasn't been validated with live NanoGPT calls**. A missing control means this plugin doesn't send it, rather than proving the provider lacks it. [Response handling and limits](tool-reference.md#nanogpt-responses-and-errors) explain the supported result shapes.

## Compatibility and recorded coverage

| Host | Support floor | Recorded coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode 1 | 1.18.29 | 1.19.3: real-agent Codex and OpenAI API runs. Floor: plugin/skill load and OpenAI API sign-in registration only. |
| OpenCode 2 | 2.0.32 | 2.0.32: real-agent Codex and OpenAI API runs. |

The Codex container runs covered skill loading and image generation before backend selection existed. OpenAI API runs covered generation and a reference edit on each host, including environment-key precedence and, in an earlier run, saved keys. Intermediate or newer host versions aren't established by those runs. The [container runbook](https://github.com/imarshallwidjaja/oc-multi-imagegen/blob/main/docs/container-testing.md) retains the recorded evidence and source identities.

The README artwork is a separate live Codex example chain, not a new container compatibility run. NanoGPT has mocked unit coverage only.

## Account access and data

Prompts and reference images go to the active provider. Calls may consume ChatGPT quota or API credit, and the plugin doesn't probe key scope or model availability beforehand. Credentials are resolved per call after permission and are never written, activated or refreshed by the plugin.

This is an unofficial integration, not an OpenAI or OpenCode product. The MIT license covers the software, not provider access or service terms.

# Development

[README](../README.md) · [Getting started](getting-started.md) · [Backends](backends.md)

## Build and check

Install dependencies with `bun install --frozen-lockfile`. The repository's normal checks are:

```sh
bun run test
bun run typecheck
bun run check
bun run build
npm pack --dry-run
```

`test` runs the mocked unit suite only. Bare `bun test` also discovers the live e2e suite, so use the package script for routine work. `check` runs Biome without rewriting files. The build produces `dist/index.js`; rebuild and restart the loading OpenCode server after source changes.

The executable commands live in `package.json` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The GitHub workflow runs frozen dependency installation, typecheck, Biome, mocked tests, build and the package dry-run.

## Package contents

The package includes the generated entry point, `server.js`, the authored skill, README, topical guides, example images, license and package metadata. The container-testing runbook and `scripts/` remain source-checkout material. Local `.tmp/`, `.hive/`, credentials and development dependencies aren't published.

The existing package test packs the checkout, extracts it, bundles the entry point into the extracted copy and checks that its skill and linked documentation resolve there. This proves relocation and asset inclusion, not runtime loading of the exact built `dist/index.js` with only production dependencies. The live container runbook covers that separate check.

## Host adapters

One default export serves both hosts. OpenCode 1 calls `server()` and OpenCode 2 calls `setup()`. OpenCode 2 checks the root `server.js` entry before the package's `main`; both entries reach the same build. Neither OpenCode SDK is imported at runtime.

Each host adapter selects the backend once and registers its declared tools. The shared image flow parses arguments, asks permission, resolves the session directory and credential, reads references, generates, checks cancellation and saves the PNG. Provider-specific schemas, model controls and requests belong to the backend.

## Bundled skill

There is one authored skill at `skills/oc-multi-imagegen/SKILL.md`. It teaches image technique; tool arguments and backend limits remain in the tool descriptions and model information.

- OpenCode 1's `config` hook adds the package's absolute `skills/` directory to `skills.paths` once, preserving existing paths and URLs.
- OpenCode 2 registers the skill through its skill transform and leaves an existing skill with the same ID alone.

Neither host gets a copied user-directory file. If OpenCode 1 finds the same skill ID elsewhere, which copy it keeps isn't defined. Missing or malformed packaged skill content fails plugin load. The tools work without loading the skill, and the plugin doesn't request skill permission.

## Live checks

`bun run test:e2e` starts its own OpenCode process and makes real authenticated image calls. It uses account quota. Run the whole file, because later cases reuse earlier outputs. Set `OPENCODE_MODEL` for the agent model or leave it unset for the host default.

For real-agent runs on both hosts, use the [container-testing runbook](https://github.com/imarshallwidjaja/oc-multi-imagegen/blob/main/docs/container-testing.md) from a source checkout. It covers Codex and the OpenAI Images API, not NanoGPT, and is an ad-hoc procedure rather than an automated CI check. It uses disposable credential seeds; never mount or print the host credential store.

Recorded compatibility evidence lives in [Backends](backends.md#compatibility-and-recorded-coverage) and the runbook. Mocked coverage, a build or a successful example doesn't establish live parity across every host, model and backend.

## Release to npm

The [publish workflow](https://github.com/imarshallwidjaja/oc-multi-imagegen/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml) runs the normal checks and publishes matching `v*` tags through npm Trusted Publishing. It uses GitHub's OIDC identity rather than an npm publishing secret. Manual **Run workflow** executions run verification only; they don't publish, even when run against a tag.

Configure the npm package's **Settings → Trusted Publisher → GitHub Actions** with user `imarshallwidjaja`, repository `oc-multi-imagegen`, workflow filename `publish.yml`, no environment name, and **Allow npm publish** enabled. The filename must match exactly. npm generates provenance automatically for this public workflow and package.

### Publish a tagged version

Update `package.json` and version-pinning examples, run the checks above, and commit the changes. The tag must equal `v` followed by the package version. For v1.0.0:

```sh
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin main
git push origin v1.0.0
```

Check the **Publish to npm** run in GitHub Actions, then verify the registry version and install it by name in a fresh directory. Later releases must use a new version and matching tag: npm versions are immutable and can't be republished. Verify a new trusted-publisher configuration with a successful publish within two days of creating it, or npm expires it.

### Manual publishing

For a manual release, run the normal checks, including the build, before creating a tarball. Confirm your npm account, then pack:

```sh
npm whoami
npm pack
```

Inspect the file list and test the generated tarball in a separate directory with only production dependencies. Import both `oc-multi-imagegen` and `oc-multi-imagegen/server`, and check that the bundled skill loads without either OpenCode SDK installed.

Publish the exact tarball you verified, using its actual filename:

```sh
npm publish ./oc-multi-imagegen-1.0.0.tgz --access public --browser=false
```

For later releases, update the package version and the tarball filename. npm versions are immutable: the same name and version can't be republished. Browser-based authentication or 2FA approval may still be required; `--browser=false` prints the URL rather than opening a browser on the publishing machine.

After publishing, verify the registry version and install it by name in a fresh directory. Keep the source changes on GitHub consistent with the published package. `ci.yml` checks the project; `publish.yml` releases tagged versions.

# A Codex image walkthrough [README](../README.md) · [Getting started](getting-started.md) · [Tool reference](tool-reference.md) The README follows one original fox postmaster through three actual Codex calls: a new scene, a reference-guided weather edit and a transparent character cut-out. The short prompts in the README are examples of what to ask an agent. This page records the longer prompts and settings used to make the displayed images. All three calls used `imagegen` with the default Codex backend. `model` and `quality` were omitted; no override is claimed to have improved the result. The output paths below are repository-relative equivalents of the temporary paths used during generation. Only those paths have been adapted. ## 1. Create the woodland post office [Full-size PNG](images/forest-post-office.png) ![The original fox postmaster and tree-house post office in warm afternoon light.](images/forest-post-office.webp) Arguments other than `prompt`: ```json { "out": "docs/images/forest-post-office.png", "size": "1672x941", "background": "opaque" } ```
Full prompt Create one exceptionally beautiful original illustration for an image-generation plugin's example gallery: a wide, cinematic, hand-painted Japanese fantasy-animation landscape with a Studio Ghibli-inspired atmosphere. An old woodland post office is built into the base of a gigantic camphor tree on a green hillside, with a moss-covered tiled roof, weathered timber walls, a tiny red postbox, warm paper windows, a narrow stone footbridge over a clear stream, ferns, white daisies and wildflowers, and distant blue mountains beneath luminous late-afternoon clouds. In the near foreground beside the bridge stands one original small anthropomorphic rust-red fox postmaster, about one fifth of the image height, with a cream muzzle, large pointed ears, a very bushy cream-tipped tail, a dark teal raincoat, a small ochre cross-body mail satchel, a tiny brass bell on the satchel and a cream envelope in one paw. Make the fox's readable silhouette and distinctive teal coat memorable, to be reused in later images. Give the scene carefully composed foreground, middle distance and background, delicate gouache and watercolor brushwork, rich botanical detail, warm honey light, cool forest greens, a quiet sense of everyday wonder, and exquisite animation-background craftsmanship. Keep the whole house, bridge and fox comfortably in frame. No written words, letters, typography, logo, signature, watermark, collage, border or user interface. No existing film characters. Make this a finished full-bleed narrative illustration, not a mockup.
The tool reported **1672x941 pixels**. The scene gives later calls a concrete character, outfit, setting and composition to follow. ## 2. Edit the scene with a reference [Full-size PNG](images/forest-post-office-rain.png) ![A reference-guided variation of the post office at rainy blue hour.](images/forest-post-office-rain.webp) Arguments other than `prompt`: ```json { "out": "docs/images/forest-post-office-rain.png", "size": "1672x941", "images": ["docs/images/forest-post-office.png"], "background": "opaque" } ```
Full prompt Image 1 is the approved original illustration: it defines the post office, giant tree, stone footbridge, fox postmaster, landscape composition and hand-painted Japanese fantasy-animation style. Recreate the same scene faithfully with the same camera position, building silhouette, bridge, distant lake and mountains, and the same rust-red fox with cream muzzle and tail tip, dark teal raincoat, ochre mail satchel, tiny brass bell and cream envelope. Apply one coherent edit: change the weather and time to a gentle rainy blue hour. Give the sky luminous indigo and lavender rainclouds, let fine rain cross the scene, add believable wet glints to the stone bridge and leaves, and make the existing paper windows and a few hanging lanterns glow warm amber against the cool forest. Add a small warm reflection in the stream. The fox remains clearly visible, cheerful and recognizable, with its envelope and outfit intact; it may now look up at the rain. Preserve the warm, tender, Studio Ghibli-inspired hand-painted animation-background craftsmanship, delicate gouache and watercolor textures, quiet everyday magic and detailed foliage. Keep all image elements in the same overall locations; do not redesign the post office or replace the character. No written words, typography, logo, signature, watermark, collage, border or interface. Deliver one finished full-bleed landscape illustration.
The tool again reported **1672x941 pixels**. The fox, building, bridge and landscape remain recognisable, while the sky, rain, reflections and lighting change. This is a regenerated variation, not a pixel-preserving local edit. ## 3. Make a transparent illustrated icon [Full-size transparent PNG](images/fox-postmaster-icon.png) Arguments other than `prompt`: ```json { "out": "docs/images/fox-postmaster-icon.png", "size": "1254x1254", "images": ["docs/images/forest-post-office-rain.png"], "background": "transparent" } ```
Full prompt Image 1 is the approved original rainy woodland-post-office illustration. Use ONLY its fox postmaster as the character reference: match the rust-red fur, cream muzzle and cheeks, large pointed ears with dark tips, generous fluffy cream-tipped tail, dark teal raincoat with small brass buttons, ochre leather cross-body mail satchel, tiny hanging brass bell, and cream envelope. Create one beautifully drawn standalone full-body illustrated mascot icon of this exact original fox, in a friendly three-quarter pose looking slightly upward, holding the envelope in one paw. It should feel like a carefully painted character cel from a Studio Ghibli-inspired Japanese fantasy animation: elegant confident silhouette, tender expressive face, richly controlled watercolor and gouache shading, a few beautiful fur strokes, readable shapes at small sizes, lovely warm russet against deep teal. Keep the character's design faithful to Image 1 while simplifying fine detail slightly for an avatar or illustrated icon. Include the complete ears, feet, tail, satchel, bell and envelope, with generous clear margin on every side of a square canvas. One character only, large and centered, no environment, no trees, no bridge, no rain, no scenery, no ground plane, no drop shadow, no circular badge, no app tile, no enclosing shape, no border, no written text, no logo, no signature or watermark. The deliverable is a clean reusable cut-out character illustration, not a screenshot or a mockup.
The output is **1254x1254 pixels**. The background argument requests a cut-out, while the reference supplies the character design. This is a raster illustration suitable for an avatar, sticker or illustrated icon; it isn't an editable vector icon. ## Transparency check The original PNG was decoded in a browser canvas and every pixel's alpha was inspected: | Alpha | Pixels | | --- | --- | | 0, fully transparent | 875,997 | | 1-254, partially transparent | 696,107 | | 255, fully opaque | 412 | The image was also viewed on warm-white and dark backgrounds. It has a real transparent background, not a painted checkerboard, and soft alpha across much of the subject. No matting, alpha correction or background removal was applied after generation. The two landscape previews are WebP copies encoded at quality 90 for display. Their linked PNG originals and the transparent icon are the bytes returned by the tool, without resizing, cropping, recolouring or compositing. The generated PNGs are included so you can inspect or reuse the full-size results. ## Try your own variation Use one of the generated images as a reference and name a specific change: another season, a different palette or a new expression. Keep your prompt clear about the role of each reference and inspect what changed. [The tool reference](tool-reference.md) covers reference limits, supported sizes and transparency behavior.

# Getting started

[README](../README.md) · [Backends](backends.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md)

The quickest path is the default Codex backend, which uses your ChatGPT sign-in in OpenCode. You don't need a separate OpenAI Images API key for it.

## Install from npm

Add `oc-multi-imagegen` to your OpenCode configuration, keeping any existing plugins. OpenCode downloads the package and its dependencies from npm when the server starts.

The support floors are OpenCode **1.18.29** and **2.0.32**; see [compatibility and recorded coverage](backends.md#compatibility-and-recorded-coverage) for what has actually been checked.

### OpenCode 1

Add the package to `plugin`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugin": ["oc-multi-imagegen"]
}
```

### OpenCode 2

Add the package to `plugins`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["oc-multi-imagegen"]
}
```

Restart the OpenCode server process that loads the plugin. If you attach a client to an existing server, restarting the client alone doesn't reload the plugin.

### Pin a version

Use `oc-multi-imagegen@1.0.0` instead of the bare package name to select that exact release. The same package-and-version syntax works in either host's array. Without a version, OpenCode resolves the npm package's current release according to its plugin loader.

## Sign in for Codex

Use OpenCode's ChatGPT sign-in for the `openai` provider. An OpenAI API key isn't sufficient for the Codex backend.

On **OpenCode 2**, choose **Codex browser (legacy)** or **Codex device code (legacy)**. The **Sign in with ChatGPT** token-sharing connection doesn't work with this image endpoint. [Backend authentication](backends.md#codex) explains the credential sources and supported methods.

Leave `OC_MULTI_IMAGEGEN_BACKEND` unset, or set it to `codex` in the server's environment. If you previously selected another backend, change that variable and restart the server.

## Make your first image

Ask the agent:

> Create a wide, hand-painted illustration of a woodland post office at sunset and save it as `images/post-office.png`.

The agent can load the bundled `oc-multi-imagegen` skill, call `imagegen`, inspect the saved PNG and use it as a reference for another image. The tool also works when the skill isn't available or permitted.

For an edit, name the existing file and the change:

> Use `images/post-office.png` as a reference. Change the scene to a rainy evening and save it as `images/post-office-rain.png`.

OpenCode may ask you to allow the image operation. For restricted agents or prompt-free operation, configure [permissions](permissions.md). Prompts and reference images go to the selected provider, and generation uses that account's image access and quota.

## Other backends

Use the [backend guide](backends.md) to configure the OpenAI Images API or NanoGPT. Settings belong in the environment of the **server that loads the plugin**, rather than in plugin options or a client shell attached to an already-running server.

For systemd, credential precedence or a sign-in error, start with [configuration and authentication](backends.md#configuration).

## Local development

Use a checkout when you want to modify the plugin. With Bun installed:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/imarshallwidjaja/oc-multi-imagegen.git
cd oc-multi-imagegen
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run build
```

Replace the npm entry with the checkout's absolute file URL: `"file:///absolute/path/to/oc-multi-imagegen"`. Use `plugin` on OpenCode 1 or `plugins` on OpenCode 2, as in the examples above. Rebuild and restart the loading server after changing source. [Development](development.md) lists the checks and packaging details.

# Permissions

[README](../README.md) · [Getting started](getting-started.md) · [Backends](backends.md)

Image calls request permission before reading credentials or references or contacting the provider. The permission action is the invoked tool's name; the resource is the active backend ID.

| Backend | Image actions | Resource |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `imagegen` | `codex` |
| OpenAI Images API | `imagegen` | `openai-api` |
| NanoGPT | `imagegen`, `imageedit` | `nano-gpt` |

A grant saved for one backend doesn't grant another. NanoGPT's `imageedit` is separate from `imagegen`.

## OpenCode 1

This deny-by-default example allows Codex or OpenAI image work and the bundled skill:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "*": "deny",
    "imagegen": "allow",
    "skill": { "*": "deny", "oc-multi-imagegen": "allow" }
  }
}
```

For NanoGPT, also add:

```json
{
  "imageedit": "allow",
  "imagegen_models": "allow"
}
```

These two entries belong inside the existing `permission` object. The local `imagegen_models` tool doesn't request permission itself, but an allow rule makes it available to a restricted agent.

To restrict `imagegen` to the OpenAI API resource, use:

```json
{
  "imagegen": { "*": "deny", "openai-api": "allow" }
}
```

## OpenCode 2

Rules go in `permissions`, with the broad rule first and the narrower ones last:

```jsonc
{
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" },
    { "action": "imagegen", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "oc-multi-imagegen", "effect": "allow" }
  ]
}
```

For NanoGPT, append allow rules for `imageedit` and `imagegen_models`. To restrict an image action to one backend, set its `resource` to that backend ID, such as `openai-api` or `nano-gpt`.

All image tools are direct tools, so allowing them doesn't require allowing OpenCode 2's `execute` tool.

## Skills and model information

The bundled `oc-multi-imagegen` skill is guidance, not an execution dependency. With image tools allowed and the skill denied, the agent can still generate using the tool descriptions. Allowing only the skill doesn't allow generation. The plugin never asks for a separate `skill` permission.

`imagegen_models` answers from the plugin's curated table. It reads no credential, reference file or provider API, and incurs no generation charge. Host-level visibility of local tools under deny-by-default rules hasn't been checked against a live NanoGPT host configuration; allow the tool explicitly.

## File access

The image permission covers the whole operation, including its output and reference paths. The plugin doesn't ask for separate file-access permissions: `out` and `images` accept absolute paths outside the project as well as relative paths.

An agent that inspects the result also needs a suitable `read` rule. Scope it to the files you intend, such as generated `*.png` files. A billed API call asks for no additional billing approval beyond the image permission, so keep image-tool access consistent with the quota you want an agent or subagent to use.

# Tool reference

[README](../README.md) · [Examples](examples.md) · [Backends](backends.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md)

The active backend owns its tool schemas. Codex and the OpenAI Images API expose `imagegen` for both generation and reference edits. NanoGPT exposes `imagegen`, `imageedit` and local model information through `imagegen_models`.

## Codex and OpenAI arguments

| Argument | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `prompt` | Description of a new image, or the change to make when references are supplied. |
| `out` | Destination path, relative to the calling session's project directory unless absolute. |
| `size` | Required. A Codex preset or native OpenAI `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, as described below. |
| `images` | Optional local reference paths, resolved like `out`. Up to five on Codex or 16 on the OpenAI Images API. |
| `background` | Optional `opaque` or `transparent`; defaults to `opaque`. |
| `model`, `quality` | Optional strings passed through. [Backend defaults and confidence](backends.md#codex) differ. |

Other arguments, including `n`, are removed by plugin validation and aren't sent. There is no image-count or output-format argument. Each call saves one PNG.

## Sizes

### Codex presets

| `size` | Aspect ratio |
| --- | --- |
| `1254x1254` | 1:1 |
| `1536x1024` | 3:2 |
| `1024x1536` | 2:3 |
| `1448x1086` | 4:3 |
| `1086x1448` | 3:4 |
| `1672x941` | 16:9 |
| `941x1672` | 9:16 |

Codex size is requested in the prompt; the request's API `size` field remains `auto`. The plugin adds a sentence naming the chosen dimensions and aspect ratio. It doesn't resize, crop or pad the result.

Recorded Codex outputs usually matched these presets, with some edges one pixel off. In a direct-request study, asking for 2048x2048 in prose still returned 1254x1254. The result message reports actual dimensions, so inspect them when exact sizes matter and resize or crop separately if necessary.

### OpenAI pixel sizes

Use native `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, for example `1536x864`. Both dimensions must be positive multiples of 16 with an aspect ratio between 1:3 and 3:1. The plugin sends the value unchanged. The API enforces model-specific pixel and edge limits.

The backend's documented guidance marks sizes above 2560x1440 as experimental and gives 3840x2160 as the maximum. Larger sizes cost more. An API rejection is reported rather than rounded or retried.

### NanoGPT sizes

NanoGPT takes `resolution` and, where the model lists it, `aspect_ratio`, rather than `size`. These are optional and model-specific. Use `imagegen_models` to get the accepted values before calling a model.

## Reference images

Pass local files in `images` and name each role in the prompt, for example: "Image 1: character design. Image 2: setting and colour palette." Files are sent in the order given.

On Codex and OpenAI, a nonempty reference list selects the image-editing endpoint. NanoGPT requires `imageedit` and an edit-model ID. The contents are uploaded to the provider.

An edit generates a new image guided by the prompt and references. It doesn't guarantee unchanged pixels outside the requested area. Use local image editing or compositing when a region must remain identical.

| Backend | Reference rules |
| --- | --- |
| Codex | Up to five local reference files. |
| OpenAI API | Up to 16 PNG, JPEG or WebP files. Each encoded data URL must be at most 20,971,520 characters. |
| NanoGPT | Local PNG, JPEG or WebP files. Counts depend on the model; the route limit is 31,457,280 bytes per file, with Seedream restricted to 10,485,760 bytes. |

FLUX's provider additionally documents references of at least 256 pixels per side and at most 16 megapixels, with downscaling above four megapixels. The plugin doesn't check those pixel constraints locally. OpenAI references are sent as `images[].image_url` data URLs; NanoGPT uses `input_references` and doesn't mix legacy image aliases.

## Transparent backgrounds

Set `background: "transparent"` for a cut-out. Prompt for one subject, complete edges and room around it; asking for transparency only in the prose doesn't set the argument.

Codex and OpenAI default to `opaque`. On NanoGPT, only the supported GPT Image 2.5 Flare pair exposes `background`, with `auto`, `opaque` or `transparent`; no default is injected.

The plugin doesn't inspect or modify alpha. Recorded Codex transparency includes soft edges and partially transparent subject pixels; in a direct-request study, many subject pixels were at alpha 252-253 rather than 255. Check on light and dark backgrounds and post-process when you need a fully opaque subject or hard matte. The [walkthrough](examples.md#transparency-check) records the example icon's actual alpha behavior.

## Output files

The saved file contains the provider's PNG bytes. Choosing an extension such as `.jpg` doesn't convert the image; it writes PNG data under that name. Non-PNG data is rejected before a directory or file is created.

An existing path is kept and the next available `-v2`, `-v3`, up to `-v999` suffix is chosen. This is best-effort collision avoidance, not an atomic operation. Give parallel calls distinct output paths.

Both hosts return `out` and `versioned` metadata. OpenCode 2 also returns structured output with that shape alongside the text. The message reports the actual pixel dimensions.

Relative `out` and reference paths follow the calling session's directory. On OpenCode 2 that can differ from the directory that loaded the plugin. Absolute paths are accepted, including outside the project; see [file access](permissions.md#file-access).

## NanoGPT inputs

- `imagegen`: required `model`, `prompt`, `out`; optional controls supported by that model.
- `imageedit`: the same, with a required nonempty `images` list.
- `imagegen_models`: list filters `operation`, `family`, `query`, or an exact `model` for detailed controls, limits and the model's input schema. An exact model can't be combined with list filters.

The image tools accept a curated set of generation/edit IDs and reject unknown arguments, unsupported controls or values, wrong-operation models, excess references and documented prompt-length violations before contacting the provider. There are no count, format, streaming or generic provider-routing arguments. Omitted controls aren't sent.

Every call asks for one image. Where the model's documented controls permit it, the request asks for PNG; all successful saves require PNG. [The model table](backends.md#generation-and-editing-models) lists the supported families.

## NanoGPT responses and errors

The plugin accepts exactly one `data` item with either inline `b64_json` or a download `url`. It refuses missing images, multiple images, both fields, pending jobs or a non-JSON body, and reports that nothing was saved and generation may already have been charged. It doesn't poll jobs, convert output formats or discard extra images to save only the first.

A download URL must use HTTPS without embedded credentials. IP literals, `localhost` and `.localhost` names, including trailing-dot variants, are refused. Public hostnames aren't checked for private-address DNS resolution. Downloads carry no API key, follow no redirects, use the call's cancellation signal and are limited to 64 MiB. An uncompressed download must match a valid declared `Content-Length`; compressed responses can have an encoded length different from their decoded body.

Provider HTTP errors include the tool, model, status, bounded error code and message, with the key removed. HTTP 5xx and transport/read failures disclose possible charges. Network diagnostics name the stage without exposing runtime messages, codes, causes, signed URLs or download hosts. A failed download or save doesn't imply the provider refunded a generation.

## Validation, permissions and cancellation

Arguments are validated before permission. Permission is requested before credentials, references or the provider are touched. Invalid reference files fail before the quota-consuming request.

Stopping a call forwards cancellation to the provider request. A result arriving after cancellation isn't saved. Failures and cancellations propagate rather than returning success, and the plugin never retries or selects another backend or model.

Provider access, account quota, balance, key scope and model availability are enforced by the selected service, not probed at startup. Check a returned error before deciding whether to correct an input or ask the operator for a decision.
